installation.note: mount is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The mount command attaches a filesystem to a directory tree, making it accessible. It's essential for accessing external storage devices, network shares, and other filesystems. Modern systems often auto-mount devices, but mount is still crucial for manual mounting and system administration.
when_to_use: Mount USB drives or external storage

syntax.description: Without arguments, mount displays all currently mounted filesystems. With device and directory, it mounts the device to the specified mount point.

options.description: Specify filesystem type (ext4, ntfs, vfat, iso9660, etc.)
options.use_case: When mount cannot auto-detect the filesystem type

options.description: Mount options (ro, rw, noexec, nosuid, etc.)
options.use_case: To mount read-only or with specific security options
During system boot or to mount all configured filesystems
To see filesystem labels when listing mounts

misconceptions.title: Auto-mounting
misconceptions.misconception: All devices need to be manually mounted
misconceptions.reality: Modern Linux systems (like Ubuntu) auto-mount USB drives and other removable media to /media or /mnt
misconceptions.tip: Check /media or /mnt directories - your device might already be mounted

misconceptions.title: Mount point creation
misconceptions.misconception: Mount command creates the mount point directory
misconceptions.reality: The mount point directory must exist before mounting. Use 'mkdir' to create it first.
misconceptions.tip: Always create the mount point directory with 'mkdir' before mounting

common_pitfalls.solution: Use 'sudo' before the mount command, or configure /etc/fstab with user option for non-root mounting

common_pitfalls.description: Cannot unmount because device is in use
common_pitfalls.solution: Close all files and directories on the mounted filesystem, or use 'lsof' to find what's using it

common_pitfalls.description: Mount fails with 'wrong fs type' error
common_pitfalls.solution: Use 'blkid' or 'lsblk -f' to identify the filesystem type, then specify with -t option

common_pitfalls.description: Mount fails because directory doesn't exist
common_pitfalls.solution: Create the mount point directory first: 'sudo mkdir -p /mnt'

related_commands.description: umount unmounts filesystems that were mounted with mount
lsblk lists block devices to identify what to mount
blkid shows filesystem types and UUIDs for mounting
/etc/fstab file defines filesystems to mount automatically

best_practices: Always use 'sudo' for mounting (unless configured otherwise)
Create mount point directories before mounting
Use 'mount' without arguments to verify mounts
Use 'umount' to safely unmount before removing devices
Verify device names with 'lsblk' before mounting
performance_tips: Mounting network filesystems can be slow - use 'mount -o soft' for better timeout handling
For read-only access, use '-r' option to improve performance

additional_notes.warning: Improper mounting can cause data loss. Always unmount before removing storage devices.
additional_notes.fstab: For permanent mounts, add entries to /etc/fstab instead of mounting manually each time
